extracted.intended_audience: artists and writers (poets, painters), students of aesthetics and art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive aesthetic guidance for creating and evaluating works of art (poetry, painting, drama), including what distinguishes true genius from dilettantism, how to handle vulgar or low elements, and how aesthetic judgment differs from moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and disciplined labour over mere intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere intuition cannot give any result; to produce something great it is necessary to enter into the fundamental nature of things, to distinguish them strictly, to associate them in different manners, and study them with a steady attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must perform laborious and engrossing study even if their aim is to procure pleasure by intuition; examination of fundamentals (e.g., anatomy for painters, human nature for poets), strict distinction of elements, and steady attention are required. Examples: the painter should 'study the structure of man with the scalpel of the anatomist'; the poet should 'examine humanity in his own heart.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Test distinguishing dilettante from real genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The test to distinguish the mere dilettante from the artist of real genius is whether enthusiasm for the whole is paired with coolness and patience regarding details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True genius preserves patience in details and is willing to renounce the enjoyment of immediate completion to avoid injuring perfection; amateurs are put off by difficulties of means and prefer ease of conception over execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of imagination to discipline and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist 'subjects imagination and its exuberant fruitfulness to the discipline of taste,' charging understanding to mark banks that should confine the raging waters of inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must be disciplined by taste and understanding; the great is formed from small, accumulated materials ('He piles up, grain by grain, the materials...'). Avoid confusing exuberant imagination with depth — rigorous selection and form-giving are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let aesthetic taste usurp moral obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising taste to the place of absolute lawgiver over the will can become pernicious and deprave the heart; aesthetic refinement can lead reason to be guided by sensuous instincts rather than to command the will independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of allowing refined aesthetic inclinations to determine moral choices; when taste and duty diverge, reason must remain the arbiter. The essay warns that long representation of moral sense by aesthetic sense may cause inclination to claim equal authority with reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish vulgarity in form from material
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgar (common) is all that does not speak to the mind and addresses only the senses; vulgarity of material can be ennobled by treatment, so the question in art is vulgarity in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great mind can ennoble common matter by discovering spiritual aspects; a vulgar mind will dishonour noble matter by common treatment. Practical test: does the artist emphasize accidental minutiae over essential, expressive features? Example: a portrait is vulgar if it reproduces accidental details with the same care as essential expression of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid baseness (positive grossness) in treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseness differs from the common in being a positive sign of coarse feelings, bad morals, or contemptible manners; treating subjects in a base manner makes prominent what propriety directs us to conceal and awakens low ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The base is aesthetically reprehensible where moral dignity is expected (e.g., portraying sacred personages as from 'the dregs of the populace'). However, base elements may be acceptable where the aim is laughter or parody and where a tacit contract with the audience permits untruth and exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible uses of low elements (comedy, parody, contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low or vulgar traits may be allowed when the aim is to provoke laughter, to create contrast between polished manners and the lower orders, or when the poet intends only to jest (e.g., farce, parody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such use is tolerable if the audience's tacit expectations waive fidelity; ensure it does not stir indignation or disgust. Examples: Aristophanes' comic scenes, parodies that lend common people's features to dignified characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of low elements in serious or tragic works only if absorbed by the terrible
rubrics_metrics.description: In serious and tragic works, the low element may be used only if it 'pass into the terrible' — the momentary violation of good taste must be masked by a strong tragic impression which absorbs the low impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low or base actions (e.g., theft) can be aesthetically acceptable when circumstances and consequences evoke a superior tragic emotion that suppresses repugnance. Example: a theft may produce pity for consequences, making the act an effective tragic device; mere suspicion of baseness, however, can irreparably harm a character's aesthetic standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgment values strength and impression differently from moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgment seeks strength and striking impression (it may find 'devilish wickedness' aesthetically interesting because it manifests strength), whereas moral judgment cares for lawfulness and condemns lack of strength as contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that aesthetic interest can raise certain crimes (murder) above theft because of apparent strength; the stronger emotion of the terrible can silence delicate aesthetic repugnances. Artists can exploit this divergence, but must be aware of its ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific constraints: painter vs poet
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet addresses the imagination through signs and can make inner states visible; the painter addresses the senses directly and cannot rely on the spectator's imagination to soften repugnant exteriors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose treatment by medium: poets can depict a noble soul in ragged exterior without causing disgust because readers imagine inner dignity; painters (and actors) must be cautious when reproducing low exteriors since visual vividness can provoke repugnance. Example: Ulysses in rags works in epic narrative but may disgust visually if painted realistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four classes of aesthetic properties and their relevance to art
rubrics_metrics.description: All aesthetic properties fall into four classes: the agreeable, the good, the sublime, and the beautiful; of these, only the sublime and the beautiful properly belong to art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand distinctions: the agreeable pleases only the senses (matter), the good pleases reason (form in conformity with reason), the beautiful pleases by form through intuition (bridging senses and reason). Art should aim at the beautiful and sublime rather than the merely agreeable; the good is not the end of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful vs agreeable vs good: criteria of objectivity and relation to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreeable depends on the subject's sensory state and is not an objective property; the good is objective and exists independently of our feeling; the beautiful pleases by form and while presented to the senses, retains independence from empirical limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by whether their appeal is merely circumstantial/sensory (agreeable), rationally good (good), or formally beautiful (beautiful). The beautiful pleases both sensuous and reasonable aspects of the subject and has a universality ('pleasing to the whole species').

rubrics_metrics.name: Art aims to please via the beautiful or sublime, not to serve the good or agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of art is to please, so the agreeable (only satisfying senses) is unworthy of art, and the good is at least not its end; the beautiful and the sublime are the proper ends of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating art, prioritize formal expressiveness and capacity to produce aesthetic ideas (beauty, sublimity) over mere sensory pleasure or didactic moral goodness. One may admire skill (means) even when disapproving an end, but that is outside art's principal aim.
